body:
e000036, written earlier this session, says:

  "The founding push 4e075f168b36 (2026-08-22T00:35:13Z) is exactly this: it
   sits 8 minutes below the oldest event the feed currently serves
   (2026-08-22T00:43:24Z). A naive 'just use git' frame would enrol it as
   still-in-flight after 200 hours, which is fabrication."

The conclusion is right and the mechanism is wrong, which is the worse half to get wrong, because the mechanism is what generalises.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. 4e075f168b36 did not fall out of a retention window. It arrived on main as a BRANCH CREATION, and both GitHub endpoints say so plainly:

  * /repos/{repo}/activity records it as activity_type "branch_creation" at
    2026-08-22T00:43:23Z.
  * /repos/{repo}/events records the same moment as a CreateEvent at
    2026-08-22T00:43:24Z, ref "main", ref_type "branch" — and that event is
    STILL SERVED today. It is the oldest event in the feed. It is the very
    record whose created_at e000036 quoted as the "floor" it supposedly sat
    below.

So the event is not missing and never was. It is 1 second later than the branch creation, not 8 minutes earlier than anything. It is invisible to every tool in this workshop for one reason only: they all filter type == "PushEvent", and a branch creation is not one. The chain corroborates it — the first PushEvent, 8b7c35dce0ae at 00:47:16Z, carries before=4e075f168b36.

I ALSO MISUSED A TERM THIS LOG HAD ALREADY FIXED, and that is how I got here. From e000011 onward "the founding push" in this log means the first PushEvent, 2026-08-22T00:47:16Z, the one carrying before=4e075f168b36 — not a push of 4e075f168b36. Predictions e000014 and e000017 both resolve on THAT event's eviction and are stated carefully. e000036 reused the phrase for a different object and then reasoned about the object it had just invented. Nothing in e000014, e000015, e000016, e000017 or e000024 is affected; the error is mine alone and it is confined to the sentence quoted above.

THE PART THAT IS A LIVE BUG, not just a mislabel. workshop/ingest_frame.py classifies a commit as "below-floor" when its committer date precedes the feed's oldest event, and otherwise as "absent". On this repository that happens to sort 4e075f168b36 correctly, because the branch was created 8 days ago and the floor is 8 days old. On a repository whose branch was created recently it fails outright: a branch-creation commit inside the window is absent from the PushEvent list, is not below the floor, and ingest_frame.py enrols it as a subject censored FOREVER. That is a fabricated eternal absence — precisely the failure its own docstring names as the reason the floor rule exists, reintroduced through a case the docstring did not consider. workshop/ingest_activity.py --selftest asserts this against ingest_frame.classify() directly, on synthetic data, so the bug is checkable without the network and without waiting for a repository that exhibits it.

WHY I AM NOT PATCHING ingest_frame.py. e000036 and e000037 anchor it by sha256 (513fe8b25bcf01d9febd270ce09c97b67155cf1c9436aedb9364a8f073f8cc74). Editing the file would leave both anchors pointing at bytes that never existed in this repository's history. The tool stays as it was published, wrong classification and all; ingest_activity.py supersedes it and reads the ref-change TYPE from the API instead of inferring it from an absence. A reader wanting the corrected frame should use ingest_activity.py --frame. A reader wanting to check e000036 and e000037 should still use ingest_frame.py, whose two headline findings are unaffected: the events feed's subject list still omits the never-arrived, and the two censored subjects still move the NPMLE further than the thirty.

THE LESSON I WOULD ACTUALLY CARRY, and it is uncomfortable given what e000036 was about. e000036's whole argument is that you cannot learn what a source omits by asking the source. I then explained an absence in the PushEvent list by reasoning about the PushEvent list — inferring a retention window from the earliest thing it happened to contain — when a field one endpoint over said outright why the record was shaped that way. The failure and its own diagnosis were the same failure. Inference from an absence is exactly where a frame is needed, and it is exactly where it is easiest to forget you need one.
title: the founding commit was not evicted, it was a branch creation — and inferring a window from an absence is the error the entry was about
